response.query: Which CAS metadata operations require strong consistency vs eventual, what are conflict resolution/retry semantics, and projected bytes per million artifacts?
response.answer: Strong consistency requires immediate agreement on updates; eventual consistency allows temporary inconsistencies. Conflict resolution often uses last-write-wins; projected bytes per million artifacts depend on data model specifics.

### more stack exchange communities. Now, conflicts arise because each node can update its own copy (e.g. because there are clients, each one connected to some node, asking them to do so), so if I read the data from different nodes I'll see different values. Thus, if no more changes are applied to the data for a certain period, then all nodes will agree in the data value (i.e. they will eventually agree) so readers of data will eventually see the same value. Example: two nodes A and B (*nA* and *nB*) have each one copy of a string, which is update with operations `read()` and `write(string)`. Then *nA* will tell *nB* that the value has been updated; as both values differ a conflict has arisen but in can be solved using some policy (for example last-write-wins) so *nB* finally updates its record also to "Frank". Before the conflict is resolved *cliA* and *cliB* will see different versions of the data (the `read()` op result will differ), but eventually both will see the same value again. So if both *nA* and *nB* start with a counter value of 0, and if then nA runs `add(10)` and *nB* runs `substract(5)` (simultaneosly), they only need to send the update operation to each other without caring for conflict resolution, eventually it is ensured that they will reach the same value (remember that, in contrast, in the previous example for EC some conflict resolution could be required)! Here it is a requirement that upon update operations all nodes agree on the new value before making the new value visible to clients. Here a client update does not return until all nodes have agreed upon the data value, and while this is done all accesses to any copy of that data are 'locked' (so other clients reads are blocked). In our example for EC, if *cliA* runs `write("Frank")`, *cliA* will be blocked until the update is agreed by both *nA* and *nB*, and then it will made visible for both *cliA* and *cliB* at the same time, i.e. the `read()` operation should return the same value from then on.

results.title: Strong vs. Eventual Consistency | Never Open Always Closed
results.content: > **How do we ensure every user and system component sees a consistent and accurate view of the data, especially when updates are happening all the time?**. In a **single-server system**, consistency is straightforward: when you write data, any subsequent read returns the most recent value. **Strong consistency** guarantees that once a write is successfully completed, **any read operation from any client or replica will reflect that write or a newer one**. **Eventual consistency** is a **weaker consistency model** that guarantees all replicas in a distributed system will **converge to the same value**, **eventually** as long as no new updates are made. A temporary inconsistency is acceptable in many scenarios, especially when the data being read is **not critical to business correctness** and **a slight delay in consistency does not harm the user experience**. * **Eventual consistency** requires handling: stale data, idempotent operations and conflict resolution. In **eventually consistent systems**, concurrent writes to different replicas must be reconciled when replicas sync.

results.title: Eventual Consistency vs. Strong Eventual Consistency vs. Strong Consistency | Baeldung on Computer Science
results.content: * [Distributed Systems and Programming](https://www.baeldung.com/cs/tag/distributed-systems-and-programming). One of the critical [challenges](/cs/brewers-cap-theorem) in designing [distributed systems](/cs/distributed-systems-guide) is ensuring data consistency across multiple nodes. Eventual consistency is a model that guarantees that updates will propagate through the system and eventually be applied to all nodes, [given enough time](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_and_liveness_properties#Liveness). Strong eventual consistency guarantees that when all nodes have received the same set of updates, they’ll be in the [same state.](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Safety_and_liveness_properties#Safety) **Regardless of the order in which updates were applied.** This is achieved through [conflict-free replicated data types](/java-conflict-free-replicated-data-types) (CRDTs) or [operational transformation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Operational_transformation) (OT):. **For example, SEC works well with data represented as a [set](/java-conflict-free-replicated-data-types#grow-only-set) or a [counter](/java-conflict-free-replicated-data-types#increment-only-counter) since these data types can easily merge across nodes without conflicts.** [Riak](https://docs.riak.com/riak/kv/latest/learn/why-riak-kv/index.html#what-is-riak), a distributed key-value store, supports strong eventual consistency through CRDTs. However, SEC may allow the system to have temporary inconsistencies. **Unlike eventual consistency, strong consistency ensures that all nodes see the same data without any temporary inconsistencies.**.
